section_title: Can we love our neighbors while choosing whom to value?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. 9 But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors. 10 Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it. 11 For He who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker.
12 Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom. 13 For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

context_lines: The royal law is stated in Scripture: love your neighbor as yourself. James does not allow favoritism to be excused as a harmless preference. It breaks that command.

The illustrations about adultery and murder explain why selective obedience is insufficient. The same God gave both commands. Keeping one does not cancel breaking the other, and a good record elsewhere does not make mistreating a poor neighbor acceptable.

The coming judgment gives speech and action their weight. James joins the law of freedom with mercy: people who need God’s mercy must take seriously their treatment of others. The warning continues the call to put the word into practice.
common_interpretation_lines: [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/james/2.htm) and [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-general-epistle-of-st-james/) both understand the commands as the will of one Lawgiver, requiring consistent love rather than selective obedience. Calvin explicitly distinguishes becoming a lawbreaker from a claim that every offense is equally serious, and both connect the judgment warning with the need to show mercy.
god_plan_lines: The command comes from [Leviticus 19:15–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/leviticus/19.htm), where fair judgment stands beside love of neighbor. James carries that concern into a community confessing Jesus.

Jesus’ account of the forgiven servant in [Matthew 18:21–35](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/18.htm) connects receiving mercy with extending it. The servant’s failure makes clear why mercy is more than polite feeling: what someone has received is meant to shape how that person treats another.
